Sister Annie

Biography

In the vibrant and meticulously preserved oral traditions of the Grenadines, the figure of Sister Annie (often immortalized as Sesé Ani) stands not merely as a single historical woman, but as a legendary ancestral archetype. Deeply entrenched in the cultural fabric of Carriacou and Petite Martinique, Sister Annie represents the profound spiritual continuity of the African diaspora in the Caribbean. Her name is synonymous with the Big Drum Dance, also known as the Nation Dance, which is one of the most unadulterated retentions of West African musical and ritualistic heritage found anywhere in the Americas. While conventional colonial archives, such as plantation ledgers or parish registries, may not offer a standard birth-to-death biography for a single definitive "Sister Annie," her life and legacy have been vividly documented through the island's indigenous musical records. She is the eponymous subject of one of the most famous and reverently performed ancestral songs in the Carriacouan repertoire. To understand Sister Annie is to understand the matriarchal power, the spiritual devotion, and the unyielding cultural memory of the people of Carriacou.

The Legend of Sesé Ani and the 1962 Recordings

Much of what the outside world knows of Sister Annie stems from the groundbreaking ethnomusicological field recordings made by Alan Lomax and his daughter Anna Lomax Wood in 1962. When Lomax traveled to Carriacou, he discovered an island that had functioned in profound geographic and cultural isolation. This unique historical circumstance allowed its people to preserve the languages, drum rhythms, and rituals of their African forebears with astonishing clarity, long after such traditions had been suppressed or syncretized on larger neighboring islands.

During these recording sessions, a prominent Big Drum lead singer—or chantwell—named May Fortune performed the traditional song dedicated to Sister Annie. Accompanied by Sugar Adams playing the lead cutter drum, and Daniel Aikens alongside Caddy Lazarus John playing the supporting boula drums, May Fortune’s commanding voice cut through the Caribbean night, etching the legend of Sister Annie into the permanent global archive of human culture.

"Sesé Ani-o, leve-o, Sesé Ani-o, leve-o, Sesé Ani-o, leve-o. No u ka wulé." (Sister Annie, wake up. Your name is ringing.)

This chorus is far more than a simple melody; it is a direct invocation of the ancestors. In the cosmology of the Big Drum, the dead are never truly gone; they remain active participants in the affairs of the living, requiring sustenance, respect, and remembrance. The phrase "leve-o" (wake up) is a plea for Sister Annie's spirit to rise, cross the waters from the ancestral realm, and join the community. The song is categorized as a song of migration, tying Sister Annie's spiritual presence to specific locations in Grenada, such as L'Abbe (modern-day Grenville) and Barcolet. Through these lyrics, Sister Annie becomes the ultimate symbol of the enduring bond between the living Carriacouans and their ancestors.

The Big Drum (Nation Dance) Tradition

To fully grasp the significance of Sister Annie, one must delve deeply into the tradition that keeps her name alive: the Big Drum, or Gwa Tambu. Originating during the era of transatlantic slavery, the Big Drum is a ritualistic complex of drumming, singing, and dancing that honors the specific ethnic "nations" from which the enslaved population of Carriacou was drawn.

When Africans were brought to the island to work on sugar and cotton plantations, they were intentionally separated from their kin to prevent uprisings. However, on Carriacou, these diverse groups—including the Kromanti (Coromantee), Igbo, Manding, Arada, Temne, and Chamba—managed to forge a shared cultural identity while meticulously preserving the distinct rhythmic cycles of their specific nations.

The Big Drum is played on three drums traditionally made from wooden rum kegs. The construction of the drums themselves is an act of historical continuity and defiance. The rum kegs were obtained from the colonial sugar trade, effectively repurposing the very tools of their exploitation into vessels of cultural liberation. The drum skins—usually from a mature male goat for the cutter drum to provide a sharp, resonant snap, and female goats for the boulas to produce a deeper, rounder tone—are cured, stretched, and secured with intricate rope tunings.

The cutter drum sits in the center, dictating the rhythm and "conversing" directly with the dancers who enter the ring. The two boula drums provide a steady, hypnotic baseline. When the chantwell begins the song for Sister Annie, the drummers lay down a specific national rhythm, and the dancers, dressed in traditional billowing skirts and petticoats, interpret the beat through highly stylized, rhythmic footwork. Sister Annie's song belongs to this sacred repertoire, ensuring that the memory of the matriarchs is physically embodied by each new generation of dancers in the ring.

Saraca Feasts and the Maroon Festivals

The invocation of Sister Annie typically occurs during highly sacred community gatherings, most notably the Tombstone Feasts and the Maroon Festivals. In Carriacou, a person’s death is not the end of their social obligation. Several years after a loved one passes, the family holds a "Tombstone Feast" or "Stone Laying" to permanently secure the ancestor's resting place and elevate their spirit to the status of a revered "old parent."

These events are centered around the Saraca, a sacrificial feast with deep West African origins. Each aspect of the Saraca is highly codified. The cooking is done communally, usually outdoors in massive iron pots over open wood fires. The community prepares large quantities of traditional foods, such as rolled rice, stewed meats, coo-coo (cornmeal), and ground provisions. The sacrifice of animals, typically sheep, goats, or fowls, is handled with utmost reverence, ensuring that blood is offered to the earth to satisfy the ancestral thirst before the meat is prepared for the living. A "parents' plate"—an unseasoned portion of the finest cuts of meat and first grains—is placed under a sacred tree or at the crossroads to feed the spirits.

It is in this spiritually charged environment, often under the light of the moon, that the Big Drum begins to play. When May Fortune and other chantwells sing "Sesé Ani-o, leve-o," they are literally calling Sister Annie and the other old parents to come and partake in the Saraca. The community relies on the satisfaction of these ancestors to bring rain, ensure a bountiful harvest, and bless the launching of new locally built boats.

The Maroon Festivals, which are community-wide celebrations held at crossroads or village centers, similarly rely on the presence of ancestral matriarchs like Sister Annie. These festivals are deeply rooted in communal sharing and the appeasement of the spirits. If the ancestors are forgotten, it is believed that hardship, drought, or misfortune will befall the island. Therefore, singing the name of Sister Annie is an act of communal survival and spiritual insurance.

"The Big Drum is not just music; it is the archive of our bloodline. When we sing for Sister Annie, we are proving that the chains of slavery could not erase our memory."

The Matriarchal Role in Carriacouan Oral History

The figure of Sister Annie also highlights the deeply matriarchal nature of cultural preservation in Carriacou. Throughout the island's post-emancipation history, men often left the island to seek work as sailors, shipwrights, or laborers on neighboring islands and in the Panama Canal Zone. This long-standing migratory pattern left the women of Carriacou as the primary heads of households, the spiritual leaders of the community, and the uncontested keepers of the oral tradition.

Women like Sister Annie—and later, women like May Fortune who sang her praises—were the chantwells. The chantwell is the ultimate authority in the Big Drum ring. She memorizes hundreds of songs in patois and various African linguistic fragments, knows exactly which drum rhythms belong to which local families (based on their ancestral "nation"), and controls the pacing of the ritual. The chantwell uses her voice to discipline the community, mourn the dead, and negotiate with the spiritual realm.

Sister Annie, therefore, is the archetype of the Carriacouan matriarch. She is the "old parent" who watches over the island, the grandmother whose name must be "rung" to maintain cosmic balance. The transmission of her song from grandmothers to granddaughters over centuries represents one of the most successful acts of cultural resistance in the Western Hemisphere.

A Lasting Legacy of Cultural Resistance

Today, the name Sister Annie remains synonymous with the unyielding pride of Carriacou and Petite Martinique. While the modern world has introduced new technologies and shifting cultural dynamics to the Caribbean, the Big Drum Dance continues to thrive, protected by a new generation of musicians and dancers who refuse to let the traditional nation rhythms die. Organizations like the Association for Cultural Equity continue to study and promote the recordings that brought Sister Annie to the world's attention.

The legacy of Sister Annie—immortalized in the grooves of Alan Lomax's 1962 recordings and kept alive in the dusty dance rings of Carriacou—proves that history is not only written in colonial books; it is sung, drummed, and danced by the people who lived it. She is a testament to the fact that the enslaved Africans of the Caribbean did not arrive as blank slates, but as people bearing complex cosmologies, profound spiritual wisdom, and an unbreakable connection to their ancestry. Whenever the rum is poured upon the earth for the Saraca, and whenever the chantwell cries out, "Sesé Ani-o, leve-o," Sister Annie wakes up, and her name rings eternally across the Grenadines.

Major Contributions

  • Sister Annie, as an immortalized ancestral figure in the Big Drum (Nation Dance) tradition, serves as the ultimate vessel for the preservation of West African heritage in Carriacou and Petite Martinique.
  • Through the famous song "Sesé Ani-o," she became the central archetype of the island's matriarchal spiritual leadership, representing the deep connections between the living community and the "old parents" (ancestors).
  • Her legacy ensures that the specific ethnic "nation" rhythms—such as the Kromanti, Igbo, Manding, and Temne—are passed down accurately from generation to generation through the sacred rituals of the Saraca feasts and Maroon Festivals.
  • Furthermore, the documentation of Sister Annie's song by ethnomusicologist Alan Lomax in 1962, passionately sung by renowned chantwell May Fortune, introduced Carriacou's pristine African cultural retentions to the global stage.
  • Sister Annie's ongoing presence in the Big Drum repertoire acts as a living archive of cultural resistance, proving that despite centuries of colonialism and the horrors of slavery, the oral history, linguistic fragments, and spiritual cosmologies of the island's matriarchs remain unbroken and vibrant today.
